title: STE Procedural Writing
description: Governs instruction length, one action per step, imperative mood, condition order, and notes.

rules.name: Keep an instruction to twenty words
rules.message: This instruction has {value} words. Use twenty or fewer.

examples.bad: Open the client config, set the retry limit to five, set the backoff to two seconds, and then restart every worker in the pool before you run the smoke test.
examples.good: Set the retry limit to five and the backoff to two seconds in the client config. Restart every worker in the pool. Then run the smoke test.

rules.fix: Split the instruction into separate numbered steps.

citation.note: The twenty-word cap depends entirely on the word-counting contract in metrics.md. A whitespace tokenizer over-counts and fires on compliant sentences, which is why sentence_words is defined before this rule is implemented. Enforced at every tier, including relaxed: a long instruction is the failure mode that costs a reader most.

rules.name: Write one instruction per sentence
rules.message: This step carries more than one instruction ("{match}").

examples.bad: Delete the stale branch and then push the new tag.
examples.good: Delete the stale branch. Then push the new tag.

examples.bad: Edit the manifest and restart the worker.
examples.good: Edit the manifest. Restart the worker.

rules.fix: Split the step so each sentence gives one instruction.

citation.note: The rule permits two actions in one sentence when they happen at the same time, which is the simultaneous-actions exception; a checker cannot detect simultaneity, so the exception is reviewer-applied. The pattern anchors on an imperative-initial line plus a coordinating connector followed by a second imperative verb from a closed list, rather than on "and" alone, which would fire on every coordinated object. Tested: both bad examples match; both good examples do not; and "Set the retry limit and the backoff in the client config" does not match, because "the" is not a verb in the list.

rules.name: Write instructions in the imperative
rules.message: This step is not in the imperative ("{match}").

examples.bad: The operator must rotate the signing key each quarter.
examples.good: Rotate the signing key each quarter.

examples.bad: It is necessary to clear the cache before the import.
examples.good: Clear the cache before the import.

examples.bad: The token should be revoked after the audit.
examples.good: Revoke the token after the audit.

rules.fix: Rewrite the step as a direct command to the reader.

citation.note: Three alternates covering the three ways a step loses its imperative: a subject plus an obligation modal, a reader-as-subject construction, and an impersonal "it is necessary to" opener. Deliberately not a general "does the sentence start with a verb" test, which needs a tagger and misfires on every legitimate descriptive sentence inside a procedure. note-block is excepted because notes are descriptive by rule and must not be imperative. Tested: all three bad examples match, all three good examples do not, and the descriptive "The worker drains the queue" does not match.

rules.name: Put the condition before the command
rules.message: The condition follows the command ("{match}"). Put the condition first.

examples.bad: Restart the worker if the queue depth is above one thousand.
examples.good: If the queue depth is above one thousand, restart the worker.

examples.bad: Clear the cache when the import completes.
examples.good: When the import completes, clear the cache.

examples.bad: Drain the queue before the worker shuts down.
examples.good: The worker drains the queue before it shuts down.

examples.bad: For headless servers, configure the permissions required by the workload before it starts.
examples.good: Before the workload starts, configure the permissions it requires on headless servers.

examples.bad: Reconcile the ledger when the import completes.
examples.good: When the import completes, reconcile the ledger.

examples.bad: Remove the lock file if the worker is stopped.
examples.good: Note that the cache expires when the import completes.

examples.bad: Archive the report before the worker shuts down.
examples.good: Verify the checksum after each download.

examples.bad: Restart the worker if the health check fails.
examples.good: Check if the worker is running.

examples.bad: Pause the job when the queue depth passes one thousand.
examples.good: Select when you want the status to expire.

rules.fix: Move the condition clause to the front and follow it with a comma.

citation.note: Issue 9 makes condition-first an obligation and then adds the comma; Issue 7 regulated only the comma, conditional on the writer's chosen order. A checker built from the older wording misses the ordering half, so this rule enforces the ordering and comma-after-leading-condition is a separate punctuation rule. Tested: every bad example matches, no good example does. Human labelling, 2026-10: every sampled finding was a descriptive sentence the procedural classifier let through ("The command requires confirmation before removing", "Fixed a crash when using") or a manner phrase ("while preserving the meaning"), so the opening word must now look like a command -- not a determiner or pronoun, not an -ed, -s, or -ing form, not the first half of a hyphenated adjective -- and "while" followed by a gerund no longer counts as a condition. Hand labels on the evaluation corpus (2026-11) showed that "Note that" sentences, "after" or "before" followed by only a noun phrase ("after each addition"), and "if" or "when" after check, verify, ask, see, determine, decide, select, choose, know, wonder, test, confirm or happens, when the word is a verb (a question or object clause, not a condition on the action; "run the test if" still matches) were not conditions on a command, so none of the three matches now. Precision on the labelled set is 43.1% (22 of 51 findings), so the rule is advisory in every profile: it no longer counts as an error, though a suggestion still lowers the score. It stays advisory until precision reaches 65% on that set; promotion is tracked in slopvac-8l4.5.32. Issue 254 (2026-11): headings and table cells are skipped (scope body-sentence); the opener must be a known command verb, or a capitalised word followed by a determiner or code span, so a noun-phrase subject ("Action reviews offer") no longer counts; a For/To/In lead-in or an Or/Then/First connective is stripped before that test; and a sentence that starts with its condition never matches. The rule no longer declares text_type: Vale ignores it, and the opener test above replaces the closed-list classifier, so Vale and the native engine now agree.

rules.name: Keep notes free of instructions
rules.message: This note gives an instruction ("{match}"). A note only gives information.

examples.bad: NOTE: Always clear the cache before you run the import.
examples.good: Clear the cache before you run the import. NOTE: The import reads the cache at startup.

examples.bad: NOTE: Do not run two imports at the same time.
examples.good: Do not run two imports at the same time. NOTE: Two imports write to the same table.

rules.fix: Move the instruction into a numbered step and leave only information in the note.

citation.note: A note that carries an instruction is a real defect and not a style point: readers skip notes, so the instruction is lost. Enforced at every tier for that reason. The pattern anchors on a note marker followed by an imperative or obligation opener, and tolerates Markdown emphasis and blockquote markers. Tested: both bad examples match, both good examples do not (the imperative sits before the marker), and "NOTE: The import reads the cache at startup" does not match.
